title: The Biggest Living Thing Isn't a Whale

lines: This is one single plant.
Its meadows stretch across more than one hundred eighty kilometres of seabed in Western Australia.
And this is a blue whale, the biggest animal that has ever lived, at the same scale.
You can barely see it.
Most people think the biggest living thing on Earth is a whale, or a giant tree.
It isn't even close.
So how can one plant cover an area about twice the size of Paris?
Is it really one living thing? And what else out there is bigger than a whale?
By the end of this video, you will see the biggest living things on Earth side by side, on real satellite images, to scale.
Chapter one. The biggest animal.
Let's start with the champion everyone knows.
An adult blue whale is usually twenty to thirty metres long.
The biggest are longer than two city buses parked end to end.
The heaviest one ever recorded was estimated at about one hundred ninety tonnes.
In our first video, we lined it up against megalodon and the giant dinosaurs.
The whale still won.
But it is not the longest animal.
In April twenty twenty, off Ningaloo in Western Australia, researchers filmed a siphonophore coiled in a giant spiral,
deep below the surface.
Its outer ring was estimated at about forty-seven metres.
Longer than the blue whale.
And it isn't one animal in the usual sense.
It's a colony of many small bodies, joined together, each with its own job: catching food, swimming, or reproducing.
So what counts as one living thing?
Keep that question in mind. It's going to matter.
So far: the blue whale is the heaviest animal, but a colony animal can be longer.
Can anything alive get much bigger?
Chapter two. The giant trees.
On land, the giants are trees.
Hyperion, a coast redwood in California, was measured at about one hundred sixteen metres tall.
Stand a thirty-metre whale on its tail next to it,
and the tree is almost four times taller.
But height isn't everything.
The biggest single tree by volume is General Sherman, a giant sequoia, also in California.
Its trunk alone is estimated to hold almost fifteen hundred cubic metres of wood.
That's about eight times the volume of the heaviest blue whale ever recorded.
Yet even these are single trees.
What if one living thing could be a whole forest?
So far: trees beat the whale on height and on volume.
But could one living thing be a whole forest?
Chapter three. The forest that is one tree.
In the mountains of Utah stands Pando, a grove of quaking aspen.
From the air, it looks like an ordinary forest.
But every trunk grew from the same roots.
Genetically, its forty-seven thousand or so stems are copies of one single individual.
Scientists call each trunk a ramet, and the whole clone a genet:
one individual, many bodies.
Pando covers about forty-three hectares.
That's around sixty football pitches.
At its widest, the clone is about two kilometres across.
Walking from one side to the other would take you around twenty-five minutes, and every tree you pass is the same individual.
Its total weight has been estimated at about six thousand tonnes.
More than thirty of the heaviest blue whales.
And it may be ancient. A study published in twenty twenty-six estimates Pando is at least twelve thousand years old.
Other scientists say that evidence is still incomplete.
Today, Pando is struggling: deer and cattle eat the young shoots
before they can replace the old trunks.
So far: a whole forest can be one living thing.
But what if most of a giant is hidden underground?
Chapter four. The humongous fungus.
In the Blue Mountains of Oregon, in the Malheur National Forest,
trees were dying in patches.
The killer was a honey fungus.
In autumn, you can see its golden mushrooms at the foot of the trees.
But the mushrooms are only the fruit.
The fungus itself is a web of dark, root-like strands, under the bark and in the soil.
Those strands are called rhizomorphs. They creep through the soil from root to root,
and the fungus slowly feeds on the trees it infects.
Scientists sampled it across the forest and tested its DNA.
One single individual had spread across about nine hundred sixty-five hectares.
That's almost ten square kilometres.
More than twenty times the size of Pando.
From how fast it spreads, they estimated it is at least nineteen hundred years old,
and possibly more than eight thousand.
For years, it was called the largest organism on Earth.
Notice the pattern. At every step, the giant got harder to see.
And the biggest one of all is hiding underwater.
So far: a single fungus covers almost ten square kilometres.
So what could be bigger, under the sea?
Chapter five. One plant, one hundred eighty kilometres.
Shark Bay, on the coast of Western Australia.
A shallow, sheltered bay at the edge of the desert, full of underwater meadows.
These meadows are seagrass. Not seaweed:
a flowering plant, with roots, leaves and flowers, that lives under the sea.
One species here is called Poseidon's ribbon weed.
Scientists sampled ten of its meadows across the bay, to see how genetically different they were.
They expected many different plants.
Instead, all but one of those meadows turned out to be the same plant. One clone.
From one end to the other, it spans at least one hundred eighty kilometres.
The researchers called it the most widespread known clone on Earth.
To picture that distance: driving it on a motorway would take you almost two hours.
Its meadows were estimated to cover about two hundred square kilometres.
That's roughly twice the size of Paris.
And it is old. From how fast this seagrass grows,
the researchers estimated it took up to about four thousand five hundred years to spread this far.
If that's right, it started growing around the time the first great pyramids were built in Egypt.
How did it get so big? Its cells carry four sets of chromosomes instead of two.
Forty, where its relatives have twenty.
The researchers think it began when two kinds of seagrass crossed,
and that the doubled genome helped it cope with the bay's salty, hot water.
It seems to set little or no seed. Instead, it grows sideways,
between fifteen and thirty-five centimetres a year, shoot by shoot, for thousands of years.
Now let's put them all on one map, to scale.
A blue whale. A football pitch. Pando.
The honey fungus.
And the Shark Bay seagrass, spanning more than one hundred eighty kilometres.
So far: one seagrass clone spans at least one hundred eighty kilometres.
So is it the biggest living thing on Earth?
Chapter six. So which is the biggest?
Here's the twist. In the Baltic Sea, in Northern Europe,
scientists found one seaweed clone at six sites spread along more than six hundred kilometres of coastline.
That's a longer spread than the seagrass.
But nobody has measured how much area it covers. Spread is not the same as size.
So the answer depends on how you measure.
Tallest: a redwood. Heaviest animal: the blue whale. Largest known area: the Shark Bay seagrass.
Remember the question from chapter one: what counts as one living thing?
Biologists say: everything that grew from one first seed is one individual, even in separate pieces.
And none of these giants is safe.
After a marine heatwave in early twenty eleven, more than a thousand square kilometres of seagrass disappeared from Shark Bay.
The giant clone was hit too.
Some of its meadows have since grown back, but nobody knows how many more heatwaves it can survive.
So here's my question: is a clone, spread over one hundred eighty kilometres, really one living thing?
Tell me in the comments.
